big: A client gets a ₹12 lakh bonus and fears a market fall. Invest it at once, or in 12 monthly instalments? Neither wins every time. Each solves a different problem.

lines: If the market rises, the lump sum does better. If it falls soon, instalments do better. I cannot know which. Instalments can help you stay calm, which is worth something. And whatever return we quote, we state the period, whether annualised, and before or after tax.

note: The four years above compound to about 5.7% a year.

opts: Lump sum can win in rises; SIP cuts entry risk
A SIP always beats a lump sum, in every case
A lump sum always beats a SIP, in every case
SIPs guarantee a profit every time, no doubt
why: A SIP does not always win.
A lump sum does not always win.

opts: Nothing at all, the average is exact

Compound growth is below the average
why: The average hides compounding. That does not match this case.

The gap is not exactly 1%. It does not fit the facts given.
The compounded rate is about 5.7% a year. This fits the facts given.

opts: The fund logo and the tagline on it
The name of the fund manager here
Period, annualised or not, and tax basis

why: A logo adds no information. That does not match this case.

q: Why do SIPs suit salaried investors?
opts: SIPs are tax-exempt in every single case
They earn monthly, cannot time markets
SIPs cannot ever lose any value at all
SIPs have zero fund costs at all, ever, anywhere
why: SIPs have no special tax exemption. It does not answer what was asked.
Monthly income matches monthly instalments. This fits the facts given.

pts: Lump sum versus SIP: no always-winner.
